speakers: The king over all the land
meta.location: The road between Ishmael and Middoni
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)
principles: Asking for others when you could ask for yourself

world_behind.title: Lamoni's first instinct is to show Ammon off
world_behind.text: Verse 1 has the church barely established and the king already wanting to bring his Nephite to his father. The Lord stops the trip in the next verse.

world_behind.title: Aaron had been in prison the whole time
world_behind.text: Verse 2 tells Ammon that Aaron, Muloki and Ammah are held at Middoni. Alma 21 supplies the account from their side. While Ammon was rising in a court, his brother was bound with cords.

world_behind.title: The father rules everything except Ishmael
world_behind.text: Alma 22:1 says so directly, and it explains why Lamoni fears him on the road. Lamoni is a regional king answering to an overlord who is also his father.

world_behind.title: The missed feast is a political charge
world_behind.text: Verses 9 and 12 have the father asking why Lamoni skipped a feast made for his sons and his people. Absence from a royal table was a public signal, and Lamoni had been unconscious for two days.

world_behind.title: The grudge goes back to Nephi
world_behind.text: Verse 13 has the father repeating the family story: he robbed our fathers, and his children come to rob us again. Six centuries later the founding quarrel is still the working explanation for every Nephite in the land.

world_behind.title: Lamanite kingship was negotiable at swordpoint
world_behind.text: Verses 23 through 27 show a king offering half his kingdom under threat and then granting the terms freely once his life is safe. The record shows the whole transaction.

world_behind.title: The jailing followed a long expulsion
world_behind.text: Verse 30 says Aaron and his companions were refused a hearing, beaten, and driven from house to house and place to place before they ever reached Middoni. Prison was the end of a run of rejections.

words.text: To win someone with agreeable speech. Lamoni proposes it as his method with Antiomno, meaning it as a favor. The record uses the word five times, and the other four sit in accounts of political conspiracy: Jared gaining half a kingdom in Ether 8, Kishkumen's faction in Helaman 1, Gadianton in Helaman 2. Lamoni's plan is described in the book's vocabulary for palace intrigue.

To recount in order, from beginning to end. Treated at 2 Nephi 1:1. Three of the record's nine uses are in Alma 18, where Ammon rehearsed the scriptures to Lamoni. Here Lamoni rehearses his itinerary to his father because he is afraid. The same verb covers a full teaching and a nervous explanation.

Falsehoods, counted as a plural noun. The form occurs nine times in this record and never in the King James Bible, and it usually appears in lists of civic sins. The father of Lamoni uses it of Nephites as a class, alongside cunning, as the reason they cannot be admitted.

To hold back from doing what you have the power to do. Ammon tells the king it is expedient that he forbear, then explains the cost of not doing so. The word carries restraint chosen while the sword is still raised.

Stood against, held ground under attack. Treated at Mosiah 12:19. The record uses it ten times, mostly of men holding a position against a crowd or an army. Here one man withstands a king's blows and then disables the arm. He made the same move at Sebus, against clubs.

Refusing to turn the head, and so refusing to be led. Treated at 2 Nephi 25:28. It is Exodus vocabulary for Israel at Sinai, used twenty times in this record and nine in the King James Bible. Mormon applies it to the people of Middoni to explain why Aaron's mission went one way and Ammon's went another.

phrases.term: Thou shalt not go up to the land of Nephi
phrases.text: The Lord's first word to Ammon in the chapter cancels a king's travel plans. Ammon has just seen a nation begin to convert, and the guidance he gets is a redirection to a jail. The reason follows in the same verse.

phrases.term: No one hath told me, save it be God
phrases.text: Ammon answers a direct question about his sources without softening it. Lamoni asked how he knew, and Ammon names revelation flatly to a man who six chapters ago had no word for God.

phrases.term: Who is one of the children of a liar
phrases.text: The father's greeting to his son includes a slur on the man beside him. The phrase appears once in scripture. It compresses the entire Nephite-Lamanite quarrel into an insult a king can throw from horseback.

phrases.term: For he feared to offend him
phrases.text: Mormon explains why Lamoni gives a full account of his movements. The new convert is still a son with a dangerous father, and the record lets that fear stand in the narrative without comment.

phrases.term: I will not slay Ammon, neither will I return to the land of Ishmael
phrases.text: Two refusals in one sentence, given to an armed overlord. Lamoni has been a believer for perhaps a week. His first recorded act of courage is disobeying his father in public.

phrases.term: It were better that he should fall than thee
phrases.text: Ammon interrupts a killing with an argument about eternal consequences. He tells the father that his son is ready to die and he is not. The appeal is to the king's own soul, made while the king is holding the sword.

phrases.term: His blood would cry from the ground to the Lord his God
phrases.text: Ammon reaches for Cain and Abel in front of a Lamanite king. He is teaching the doctrine of bloodguilt to a man who has never heard Genesis, using it as the reason to lower a weapon.

phrases.term: Even to half of the kingdom
phrases.text: The oath a frightened monarch swears. Ahasuerus says it to Esther three times (Esth. 5:3), and Jared's daughter uses the same currency in Ether 8:10. In every case a king under pressure names the largest thing he owns, and what the petitioner asks for next is the test.

phrases.term: I will govern him no more
phrases.text: The father grants more than Ammon demanded. Independence for Lamoni's kingdom was never on the table; the request was that Lamoni be left alone. Astonishment at being spared produced the concession.

verses.label: v. 2–5
verses.title: A question is staged so the source can be named
verses.text: The voice of the Lord redirects Ammon and supplies three names in prison before anyone has asked for help. Lamoni then puts the question the reader would put: "Who told thee that thy brethren were in prison?" The answer is an attribution and nothing else: "No one hath told me, save it be God." The record sets up the exchange rather than simply reporting the revelation, and gets the provenance said out loud.

verses.label: v. 11–12
verses.title: The fear is reported before the speech is
verses.text: Lamoni "rehearsed unto him whither he was going, for he feared to offend him," and explained why he had missed the feast. The record gives his calculation first and its outcome second: "behold, to his astonishment, his father was angry with him." What is recorded is not the conversation but the gap between what Lamoni expected of it and what it produced.

verses.label: v. 13
verses.title: The grievance is property, and it is inherited
verses.text: The old king's charge runs backward and forward without a break: "he robbed our fathers; and now his children are also come amongst us that they may, by their cunning and their lyings, deceive us, that they again may rob us of our property." Robbed our fathers occurs once in scripture. It is the tradition Mosiah 10:12 sets out as the Lamanite inheritance, and here it is spoken by a king who is about to draw a sword over it.

verses.label: v. 24
verses.title: Offered everything, he itemizes three things
verses.text: Ammon's terms are a release, a throne, and a temper: the brethren out of prison, that "Lamoni may retain his kingdom," and that the father "be not displeased with him, but grant that he may do according to his own desires in whatsoever thing he thinketh." The third item on the record's list asks for nothing material at all. It asks that a son be left alone.

verses.label: v. 29–30
verses.title: The men the chapter is about never speak in it
verses.text: Aaron, Muloki and Ammah are named at verse 2 and appear again only as a condition: naked, skins worn, "bound with strong cords," hungry, thirsty, "patient in all their sufferings." The record supplies their sufferings and their patience, and no word of theirs. Strong cords ties the scene to Alma 14:4, where the same binding held Alma and Amulek.

chapter.title: The revelation comes as a schedule change
chapter.text: Ammon receives no doctrine in this chapter. He is told where not to go and where to go instead, and both halves turn out to matter. Guidance arrives as an itinerary.

chapter.title: Ammon leaves a revival to open a jail
chapter.text: The church of Alma 19 is days old and he walks away from it for three men in prison. The record shows no deliberation about whether the larger work justified staying.

chapter.title: Lamoni's conversion is tested on his father first
chapter.text: The conversion at Alma 19:13 is followed within one chapter by three costs, all quoted. Verse 15 is the refusal, "I will not slay Ammon, neither will I return to the land of Ishmael." Verse 16 is the armed parent, "he drew his sword that he might smite him to the earth." Verse 24 has the throne threatened, and verse 27 has the father revoke the threat only after Ammon declines half the kingdom. The record gives the new believer no settled interval at all between the conversion and the test.

chapter.title: Ammon fights defensively and negotiates from strength
chapter.text: He blocks the blows and disables the arm, taking no life. Then he holds the advantage long enough to get terms, and every term he asks for belongs to someone else.

chapter.title: The offer of half a kingdom is refused in effect
chapter.text: Ammon could have taken territory. He asked for three prisoners, his friend's throne, and peace between a father and a son. The king's astonishment in verse 26 is at the smallness of the demand.

chapter.title: Mercy is what converts the old king
chapter.text: He was unmoved by argument and moved by being spared, and by watching a Nephite love his son. Verse 27 has him asking to hear the words for himself, which is where Alma 22 begins.

chapter.title: The two missions are compared without ranking them
chapter.text: Ammon has a court, a queen, and a church; Aaron has cords and hunger. Verse 30 attributes the difference to the people, and calls the prisoners patient in all their sufferings.

chapter.title: The chapter runs on family quarrels
chapter.text: Four family moves run in eleven verses. Verse 13 is the insult, "these Nephites, who are sons of a liar." Verse 14 is the order, that Lamoni "should slay Ammon with the sword." Verse 16 is the drawn sword. Verse 17 is the intervention, and its argument is about the father rather than the son, "it were better that he should fall than thee... if thou shouldst fall at this time, in thine anger, thy soul could not be saved." Verse 19 records the father conceding the point, "I know that if I should slay my son, that I should shed innocent blood." A six-hundred-year national feud is argued out between two men on a road.

applications.title: Let the plan be overruled
applications.text: Lamoni's trip to show Ammon to his father was generous and it was cancelled, "Thou shalt not go up to the land of Nephi," and replaced with a rescue at Middoni. A good intention is not the same as the right errand, and the record has the redirection arrive before the trip begins.

applications.title: Go get the people nobody is counting
applications.text: The reason given for the change is three men in a cell, "thy brother Aaron, and also Muloki and Ammah are in prison," and Ammon's answer is immediate, "I go that I may deliver them." The alternative was a royal introduction.

applications.title: Use the relationship you have
applications.text: Lamoni's contribution is not power but acquaintance, "the king of the land of Middoni, whose name is Antiomno, is a friend unto me." Knowing somebody is a resource worth offering, and offering it is often the whole of what you can do.

applications.title: Argue for the other person's interest
applications.text: Ammon's case to the armed father is about the father: falling "in thine anger" would cost his soul, and killing an innocent son would bring blood crying from the ground. Neither sentence is about Ammon's safety.

applications.title: Concede the point out loud when it lands
applications.text: The father answers his own accusation, "I know that if I should slay my son, that I should shed innocent blood; for it is thou that hast sought to destroy him." Saying the concession is what ends the scene; thinking it would not have.

applications.title: Ask for less than you could
applications.text: Ammon holds a sword over a man who offers half a kingdom and asks only that three prisoners be released. Verse 26 records the effect of the restraint, "when he saw that Ammon had no desire to destroy him... he was astonished exceedingly."

applications.title: Look at what the release actually cost them
applications.text: The record does not report the rescue as a success and stop. It describes the men: naked, skins worn from the cords, having "suffered hunger, thirst, and all kinds of afflictions." Finish an account of a deliverance by saying what the people came out with.

applications.title: Assume the difference was the ground, not the worker
applications.text: The record explains the failure at Middoni by where they landed, "it was their lot to have fallen into the hands of a more hardened and a more stiffnecked people." Before concluding you did it wrong, ask what field you were in.

questions.text: What good plan of mine has been redirected, and did I treat the redirection as a loss?
How plainly do I name where my convictions actually came from?
Whose displeasure still shapes what I say about my beliefs?
What would it cost me to refuse an instruction from someone who has power over me?
When I want someone to stop, do I argue from my interest or from theirs?
When I have had the advantage, what did I ask for?
Whose patient suffering have I only found out about later?
